title: The flight
hook: the palace asleep, the gates opening, the horse's hooves muffled (Buddhacarita 5)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the plowed field, and your line: grief for the small. Did you look down once and let a small life be real? Today, night falls on the palace. Day seven hundred six.

Before he leaves, he asks. That's the part of the flight that's easy to forget. The prince comes back from the field and goes to his father, bows, and says it out loud: let me go and become a wanderer. The king weeps. Not yet, he says. You're young. Wait. Then the prince makes an offer. Promise me four things, and I'll stay: that my life won't end in death, that sickness won't take my health, that age won't take my youth, that misfortune won't take what I have. The king can't promise any of them. Nobody could. And so the asking ends, and the night begins.
screen: `FIRST, HE ASKS.` → `PROMISE ME FOUR THINGS.` → `NO ONE COULD.`

segments.voice: First, the sleeping palace. Back in his rooms, the women play music for him as always, but the poem says the gods send a heavy sleep over them, and they fall where they are, instruments still in their arms. Year one stood in that room. Tonight the poem only passes through it on the way to the door. Second, the horse. The prince wakes Chandaka, his attendant, and asks for Kanthaka, his horse. And Chandaka brings him. The prince speaks to the horse as to a friend, asking him to carry him well this one time. Third, the gates. All his life this palace has been a machine for keeping the prince in and the world out. Heavy doors. Bars. Guards. And tonight, the poem says, the gates that took strength to move swing open by themselves, without a sound. The city sleeps on. Fourth, the look back. Outside the city, the poem has the prince turn toward it and make a vow: he won't come back into this city until he has seen the far shore of birth and death. Then he rides on into the dark. Here's the arc of the last days. A father built walls. A cleared road, a garden, a friend's advice, a palace full of music. One by one, they gave. Tonight, the last one does. The gates open.
screen: `THE PALACE FALLS ASLEEP.` · `CHANDAKA BRINGS THE HORSE.` · `HEAVY GATES, OPENING ALONE.` · `A VOW TO THE FAR SHORE.` · then, large: `THE GATES OPEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: move quietly for a minute. Stand if you can, or stay seated and move just your hands. Then move as if everyone in the house were asleep. Slow. Soft. Set each foot down so it makes no sound. Lift a cup and set it down without a click. Notice how much attention quiet takes, and how the room seems to get bigger when you stop making noise in it. When the minute's done, sit, and rest in the hush you made. The bell holds the time.
The flight. The prince asks his father first, is refused, then leaves at night on Kanthaka with Chandaka, through gates that open on their own. Today's word.
Your line: the gates open. Today, notice one door you've been waiting on, and ask whether you've said out loud what you need. Day seven hundred six.

howItsDone: The prince's leaving, often called the great going forth, is remembered in Buddhist art and at festivals, and in Theravada countries young men about to ordain sometimes ride in procession on a horse or are carried, recalling the prince's ride out of the city.

match.prompt: the night of the flight: tap the pairs.

myth: in the poem, the prince slips away without ever asking his father
he asks first, and offers to stay if the king can promise him four things.
the king promises the prince he will never grow old
he can't promise it. no one could.
in the poem, the gates open without a sound
the doors that kept the world out open on their own.

fork.setup: you're the prince. you've decided to leave, but your father loves you and rules the palace. what do you do first?
options: go to him and ask, out loud.
ask a friend to decide for him.
fork.reveal: he asks his father. the king refuses, and the prince offers to stay if he can be promised he won't die, sicken, age or lose what he has.

trapdoor: what you thought: the prince ran away in secret.
what it means: in the poem he asks his father first, and leaves only when no one can promise him freedom from death.
what a scholar hears: Ashvaghosha frames the leaving as an argument lost by the king, so the night ride follows a refused request, not a whim.

sources.ref: Buddhacarita 5 (the request to the king, the sleeping palace, the departure)

notes: All Buddhacarita material paraphrased (Cowell 1894 not on the validator list).

The 'four things' count comes from the poem's request (life not ending in death, health not taken by disease, youth not taken by age, prosperity not taken by misfortune); confirm in Cowell canto 5 that there are four and in that sense.

Muffled hooves: the outline places them in Buddhacarita 5. The script says 'in the telling'; confirm whether the poem has this (some tellings have yakshas or gods bearing up the hooves) or whether it comes from the Nidanakatha/Lalitavistara.
Confirm the gates opening by themselves noiselessly, the prince addressing Kanthaka, and the vow not to re-enter Kapilavastu until he has seen the further shore of birth and death.
howItsDone describes the Theravada ordination procession recalling the going forth; confirm, or cut to the first clause.
Editor: muffled hoofbeats cut (not confirmed in Buddhacarita 5); the wonder-or-picture readings angle cut (fourth repeat in this run); 'for years' changed to 'all his life'.

Auditor (2026-10-01): 'his charioteer, Chandaka' implied he is the unnamed charioteer of the sights in canto 3; in the poem Chandaka is the horse attendant/groom (later tellings merge the two). Now 'his attendant'; confirm Cowell's term.
